text:
Blood alcohol concentration (BAC) measures the amount of alcohol in a person's body.

Most fully licensed drivers must have a BAC below 0.05.

This also applies to most people supervising learner drivers.

Police can check a driver's BAC during roadside alcohol and drug testing.

These laws apply on both public roads and private property.

section: Drivers who must have zero BAC
text:
A driver must have a BAC of 0.00 if they:
- hold a learner permit
- hold a probationary licence, including P1 or P2
- have a driver's licence or learner permit with a Z or I condition
- are a restricted motorcycle rider with an E condition
- are a driving instructor
- drive a bus or commercial passenger vehicle, such as a taxi
- drive a rigid or articulated truck greater than 4.5 tonnes gross vehicle mass

For these drivers, driving with a BAC above 0.00 is an offence.

Victoria Police conduct random roadside breath testing.

It is an offence to:
- fail to stop at a booze bus or random breath-testing station
- refuse to provide a breath or blood sample
- fail to cooperate with police conducting a breath or blood test

Refusing a breath test can result in serious penalties.

A person must not drink alcohol while:
- driving a motor vehicle
- sitting beside and supervising a learner driver

This applies even if the driver's or supervisor's BAC remains below their legal limit.

Passengers may drink alcohol in a vehicle, although doing so may distract the driver.

Alcohol can reduce a driver's ability to:
- concentrate
- make decisions
- react quickly
- judge speed and distance
- perform multiple tasks
- maintain coordination and balance

Alcohol can also cause drowsiness and increase risky behaviour.

A BAC of 0.05 is associated with approximately double the crash risk compared with a BAC of zero.

Alcohol may remain in the body the following day.

Cold showers, exercise, coffee, fresh air or vomiting do not reduce the amount of alcohol in the bloodstream.

Drivers, especially those who must maintain a zero BAC, should consider whether alcohol consumed the previous night may still affect their ability or legal eligibility to drive.

section: Mixing alcohol with drugs and medicines
text:
Alcohol should not be combined with drugs or medicines when driving.

This includes:
- prescription medicines
- medicines bought from a pharmacy or supermarket
- illicit drugs

Combining alcohol with other substances can further reduce a person's ability to drive safely.
Victorian laws concerning driving with alcohol and drugs are contained in Part 5 of the Road Safety Act 1986.

Demerit points are penalty points recorded against a driver's record when they commit certain driving offences.

The number of demerit points a driver can receive before reaching their limit depends on the type of licence or permit they hold.

### Learner and probationary drivers

The following drivers have a limit of:

- 5 demerit points in any 12-month period, or
- 12 demerit points in any 3-year period

This applies to:
- learner permit holders
- P1 probationary licence holders
- P2 probationary licence holders
- overseas licence holders with no Victorian licence who are under 22 years old

### Full licence and other drivers

The following drivers have a limit of:

- 12 demerit points in any 3-year period

This applies to:
- full driver licence holders
- other licence categories listed by Transport Victoria
- overseas licence holders with no Victorian licence who are 22 years old or older

If a driver reaches or exceeds their demerit point limit, action may be taken against their licence or learner permit.

Depending on the driver's circumstances, this may include:
- licence or learner permit suspension
- an extended demerit point period
- disqualification from driving

It is against the law to drive while a licence or learner permit is suspended or while the driver is disqualified.

Demerit points are recorded against a driver's driving record.

Drivers can check their current active demerit points using their myVicRoads account or the myVicRoads app.

source_title: Learner and probationary driver road rules
text:
As a learner driver, you must:
- carry your digital learner permit, learner permit card or receipt every time you drive
- drive with a supervising driver who has a full and current licence
- have a zero blood alcohol concentration (BAC) at all times when you drive
- not tow a trailer, caravan or another vehicle
- not operate portable devices in any way while driving, including for phone calls and navigation

source_title: Learner and probationary driver road rules
text:
Learner drivers must have a supervising driver in the front passenger seat at all times while driving.

The supervising driver must have an Australian or overseas driver’s licence that:
- is current and full, not probationary
- allows them to drive the type of vehicle being driven by the learner

When supervising a learner driver, the supervising driver must:
- carry their digital driver licence or driver licence card
- have no more than 0.05 BAC for regular drivers
- have 0.00 BAC if they are an authorised driving instructor or have a Z condition on their licence
- complete the required supervising-driver and declaration sections of the learner driver’s logbook

source_title: Learner and probationary driver road rules
text:
A P1 driver must:
- carry their digital driver licence or driver licence card when driving
- display red P plates visible from at least 20 metres away at the front and rear of the vehicle
- have a zero blood alcohol concentration (BAC)
- drive an automatic vehicle if an A condition applies to their licence

A P1 driver cannot:
- carry more than one peer passenger aged 16 to under 22, subject to listed exceptions
- operate portable devices while driving, including for phone calls and navigation
- tow another vehicle or trailer except in specified circumstances
- drive a probationary prohibited vehicle unless an exemption or other listed exception applies

source_title: Learner and probationary driver road rules
text:
A P2 driver must:
- carry their digital or P2 licence card when driving
- display green P plates visible from at least 20 metres away at the front and rear of the vehicle
- have a zero blood alcohol concentration (BAC)
- drive an automatic vehicle if an A condition applies to their licence

A P2 driver cannot:
- operate portable devices while driving, including for phone calls and navigation
- drive a probationary prohibited vehicle unless an exemption or other listed exception applies

The Road Safety Road Rules 2017 are the official statutory road rules for Victoria.

The Victorian Legislation website lists the current in-force version as effective from 18 February 2026.

This source is used as the primary legal reference for Victorian road rules.

It can be used to verify rules described in explanatory sources from Transport Victoria and VicRoads.

The legislation covers areas including:
- speed limits
- traffic signs and road markings
- intersections
- giving way
- overtaking
- stopping and parking
- pedestrians
- cyclists
- use of lights and warning devices
- road-user behaviour
- other traffic and road-safety requirements

Where a Transport Victoria or VicRoads page provides a simplified explanation of a road rule, the relevant provision in the Road Safety Road Rules 2017 can be used as the authoritative legal reference.

For questions requiring a precise legal rule, the relevant rule number and legislative text should be retrieved from the current in-force version.

source_title: Device rules for new and young drivers and motorcyclists
text:
These rules apply to:
- learner drivers
- P1 drivers
- P2 drivers
- motorcyclists who hold an E (restricted) motorcycle licence

source_title: Device rules for new and young drivers and motorcyclists
text:
A learner, P1 or P2 driver must not use a mobile phone or portable device for any function while driving unless they pull over and park.

While driving, they must not:
- use or touch a mobile phone or portable, wearable or mounted device, including for phone calls or navigation
- use voice controls to operate a device
- enter information, text, numbers or symbols
- scroll through content
- view messages, social media, emails or photos
- watch videos, play games or take video calls
- place a device on their lap or body, except in a pocket or holding pouch
- pass a device to a passenger or take one from a passenger

source_title: Device rules for new and young drivers and motorcyclists
text:
Portable devices include loose or unmounted:
- mobile phones
- tablets
- laptops
- media players
- game consoles

A driver must not:
- touch a portable device, whether it is turned on or off
- use a portable device, including through voice controls
- look at another person's device screen
- have ongoing activity on a portable device, even if navigation or audio was set up before driving
- keep a portable device on their lap or body, except in a pocket or holding pouch

To operate a portable device, the driver must pull over and park.

source_title: Device rules for new and young drivers and motorcyclists
section: Mounted devices and in-built vehicle systems
text:
A mounted mobile phone or tablet must be secured using a commercially designed holder.

A learner, P1 or P2 driver must not:
- scroll or enter information on a mounted or in-built device
- use voice controls
- use the device for messages, social media, emails or websites
- use the device for video calls

They may:
- use a mounted device for navigation or audio if it is set up before the journey starts
- briefly touch an in-built vehicle device to adjust navigation, climate controls or audio functions

A mounted device must not be touched during the drive, including while stopped at traffic lights. The driver must pull over and park to change the address or audio settings.

source_title: Device rules for new and young drivers and motorcyclists
text:
Wearable devices include:
- smartwatches
- smart glasses
- wearable head-up displays

A driver must not:
- touch a wearable device
- use voice controls to operate it
- look at the screen of a wearable device being used by another person

Audio may continue if it was set up before driving. The driver must pull over and park before touching the device or changing its settings.

source_title: Device rules for new and young drivers and motorcyclists
text:
Motorbike helmet devices include:
- communicators
- head-up displays
- cameras
- built-in or secured mobile phones

Learner and probationary motorcyclists may use these devices for navigation or audio only if the function is set up before riding.

They must not touch the device or use voice controls while riding. Any changes must be made after pulling over and parking.

source_title: Device rules for drivers with a full licence
text:
Drivers with a full licence can use a mobile phone or device to:
- make or receive a phone call
- use audio and music functions
- use GPS navigation
- use in-built driver assistance or vehicle safety features

The device must be properly mounted or built into the vehicle.

Fully licensed drivers must not touch or use an unmounted mobile phone or device while driving or riding.

While driving, riding or operating a vehicle, a driver must not:
- enter information, text, numbers or symbols, unless using voice control
- scroll through content such as text messages, social media or music playlists
- view text messages, social media, emails, websites or photos
- watch videos, play games or take video calls

These rules apply to portable, wearable, mounted and in-built devices.

source_title: Device rules for drivers with a full licence
text:
Portable devices include unmounted or loose:
- mobile phones
- tablets
- laptops
- media players
- game consoles

While driving, a fully licensed driver must not:
- touch a portable device, whether it is on or off
- operate it using voice
- look at the screen of a device being used by another person
- place the device on their lap or body, except in a pocket or attached pouch
- pass a device to a passenger or receive one from a passenger

A passenger must not pass a portable device to the driver.

A fully licensed driver may:
- connect a portable device to the vehicle's wireless technology before driving and place the device out of sight and reach
- use a portable device to pay at a drive-through
- use a CB radio or another two-way radio

source_title: Device rules for drivers with a full licence
section: Mounted devices and in-built vehicle systems
text:
A mobile phone or tablet is considered mounted when it is secured using a commercially designed and manufactured holder.

Mounted devices and in-built vehicle systems may be used for functions such as music and maps, provided the driver does not enter text, scroll, view images or play videos.

While driving, the driver must not:
- use the device for video calls

The driver may briefly touch a mounted or in-built device to:
- initiate, accept or reject an audio call
- play or stream audio
- adjust volume
- use navigation
- use driver-assistance or vehicle-operation functions
- use functions that monitor driver behaviour or condition
- perform a professional driving task

source_title: Device rules for drivers with a full licence
text:
Wearable devices include:
- smartwatches
- smart glasses
- wearable head-up displays

While driving, a driver must not:
- touch the wearable device, except for incidental contact caused by wearing it
- use it for video calls
- use its navigation function
- use functions that monitor driver behaviour or condition
- perform a professional driving task using it

Using voice controls, the driver may:
- initiate, accept or reject an audio call
- play or stream audio
- adjust volume

source_title: Device rules for drivers with a full licence
text:
Motorbike helmet devices include:
- communicators
- head-up displays
- cameras
- in-built or secured mobile phones

A rider may briefly touch the device or use voice commands to:
- initiate, accept or reject an audio call
- play or stream audio
- adjust volume
- use driver-assistance functions
- use navigation
- use functions that monitor rider behaviour or condition
- perform a professional driving task

Earbuds may also be used if the phone is mounted and used hands-free.

source_title: Driving with your overseas licence in Victoria
section: When an overseas licence can be used
text:
A person can use their overseas licence to drive in Victoria if:
- the licence is current
- the licence is valid for the type of vehicle being driven
- they plan to live and drive in Victoria for less than 6 months

The 6-month period starts from the day the person starts living in Victoria.

Leaving Victoria and returning does not restart the 6-month period.

If a person wants to drive in Victoria for more than 6 months, they must convert their overseas licence to a Victorian licence.

source_title: Driving with your overseas licence in Victoria
section: When an overseas licence cannot be used
text:
A person cannot use their overseas licence to drive in Victoria if:
- they have been disqualified or suspended from driving or obtaining a licence or permit in any country
- they have failed a driving test in Victoria
- they already hold an Australian driver licence or permit from another state or territory

source_title: Driving with your overseas licence in Victoria
text:
Drivers should carry their overseas licence when driving in Victoria.

If the overseas licence is not in English, the driver must also carry either:
- an English translation of the licence, or
- an international driving permit in English

source_title: Driving with your overseas licence in Victoria
text:
If an overseas licence is not in English, it must be supported by an appropriate English translation or international driving permit.

For licence conversion, VicRoads states that translations may need to be completed by a NAATI-accredited translator or the relevant country's consulate in Australia.

source_title: Driving with your overseas licence in Victoria
text:
A person who moves to Victoria and intends to live there for more than 6 months must convert their overseas driver licence or learner permit to a Victorian licence.

The exact conversion requirements depend on factors such as:
- the type of licence
- the person's age
- how long they have held the overseas licence
- the country or jurisdiction where the licence was issued

source_title: Driving with your overseas licence in Victoria
text: Anyone driving with an overseas licence in Victoria must understand and follow Victorian road rules.

Drivers and riders must follow the speed limit shown on signs.

If there is no speed limit sign, the applicable default speed limit must be followed.

Drivers must travel at or below the speed limit and should also drive to the road and traffic conditions.

Different speed limits may apply depending on the road environment.

Examples include:

- 10 km/h in some areas where pedestrians have priority
- 20 km/h in some car parks and recreational areas where vehicles and pedestrians mix
- 30 km/h in some areas with high pedestrian, cycling or other active-transport activity
- 40 km/h in activity centres, some school zones and local streets
- 50 km/h on many urban roads and unsigned local streets in built-up areas
- 60 km/h on some higher-movement urban roads
- 70 km/h on some divided urban arterial roads and semi-regional urban roads
- 80 km/h on some high-movement roads and rural roads
- 100 km/h on many highways and rural roads
- 110 km/h on some freeways, motorways and tollways in non-built-up areas

These are examples only. Drivers must follow the speed limit that applies to the specific road.

section: Default speed limits when no sign is displayed
text:
Where there is no speed limit sign, a default speed limit applies.

### Built-up areas and neighbourhoods

The default speed limit is 50 km/h.

This applies to roads in suburban or built-up areas where no speed limit sign is displayed.

### Country roads

The default speed limit is 100 km/h.

This applies to roads outside built-up areas where no speed limit sign is displayed.

Drivers must travel at or below the speed shown on the applicable speed limit sign.

Different types of speed limit signs may be used, including:
- standard speed limit signs
- time-based signs
- variable electronic signs
- temporary speed limit signs

Temporary speed limits may apply around roadworks.

When approaching a roadworks speed sign, a driver must:
- slow down to the speed shown on the temporary sign
- travel at or below that limit
- continue following that limit until passing a sign showing a different speed limit

The temporary speed limit still applies even when roadworks or workers are not visibly present.

section: Emergency, law enforcement and incident response scenes
text:
Drivers must slow down when passing certain stationary or slow-moving emergency, incident-response or roadside-assistance vehicles displaying flashing lights or sounding an alarm.

Drivers must:
- safely slow to 40 km/h
- pass the scene at 40 km/h and be able to stop if directed
- return to the normal legal speed limit after reaching a safe distance from the scene

Victorian speed-limit rules are contained in Part 3 of the Road Safety Road Rules 2017.

Relevant rules include:
- Rule 20 — Obeying the speed-limit
- Rule 21 — Speed-limit where a speed-limit sign applies
- Rule 22 — Speed-limit in a speed-limited area
- Rule 24 — Speed-limit in a shared zone
- Rule 25 — Speed-limit elsewhere

Drivers and riders may receive fines and demerit points for exceeding the speed limit.

More serious speeding offences may result in additional penalties such as licence suspension or cancellation and vehicle impoundment or immobilisation.
